title: Salivary Autoantibodies and Periodontitis-Associated Bacteria as Non-Invasive Biomarkers for the Diagnosis of Rheumatic Diseases
summary:
Rheumatic diseases such as Sjögren’s syndrome (SS), axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA, formerly known as ankylosing spondylitis), and particularly rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are characterized by the formation of specific autoantibodies that serve as diagnostic markers. Conventional diagnostic procedures are predominantly based on invasive blood tests, the sensitivity of which is often sufficient only once clinically manifest symptoms have developed. Against this background, the analysis of saliva is becoming increasingly important, as it provides a non-invasive medium for identifying potential biomarkers and may therefore enable the early detection of autoimmune processes.
A particular focus of research is the relationship between RA and periodontitis (PA). Epidemiological and experimental data indicate a bidirectional association involving both systemic inflammatory mechanisms and direct microbiological interactions. Central to this relationship are the periodontal pathobionts Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, which may contribute substantially to the initiation and maintenance of autoimmune processes through their ability to promote protein citrullination. Citrullination is a post-translational modification in which the amino acid arginine is converted into citrulline by peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD). Under physiological conditions, this mechanism modulates protein structure and regulates immune responses without causing pathological consequences. However, in the context of chronic inflammation or bacterial stimulation, citrullination may become pathological because the resulting citrullinated proteins can act as autoantigens and induce the formation of anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA). These autoantibodies play a central role in the destruction of joint and periodontal tissues and therefore represent a key mechanism in RA pathogenesis. At the molecular level, the PAD enzyme of P. gingivalis is localized on the outer cell membrane. Gingipains, cysteine proteases that release arginine residues and thereby facilitate PAD-mediated citrullination, are located in its immediate vicinity. In addition, A. actinomycetemcomitans can modulate PAD activity, resulting in a synergistic effect. Citrullination alters the charge and conformation of the affected proteins, causing them to be recognized as foreign by the immune system. Whereas immune tolerance is maintained under physiological conditions, this mechanism leads to a pathological autoimmune response against citrullinated proteins in RA.
To date, it has not been conclusively established whether additional periodontal bacteria, such as Fusobacterium nucleatum and Tannerella forsythia, also play a role in the pathogenesis of RA. However, there is established evidence that periodontal pathobionts such as P. gingivalis and A. actinomycetemcomitans are detected significantly more frequently in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Furthermore, patients with RA and periodontitis often exhibit higher disease activity than patients with RA without periodontitis, as reflected, among other factors, by elevated inflammatory markers such as CRP and ESR and higher ACPA and RF levels. Increased epithelial and mucosal permeability weakens immune tolerance toward microbial components and may facilitate the migration of immune cells to the joints after they enter the bloodstream through low-grade bacteremia. DNA from P. gingivalis, T. denticola, P. intermedia, T. forsythia, and F. nucleatum, as well as elevated antibody titers, has been detected in the synovial fluid of patients with RA. In addition to microbial and immunological factors, it is becoming increasingly apparent that systemic and lifestyle-related factors—particularly diet—may influence the composition of the oral microbiota and the activity of chronic inflammatory diseases such as RA. In recent years, research in periodontology has demonstrated that considering individual clinical or microbiological parameters in isolation does not adequately reflect the complexity of inflammatory diseases.
The introduction of the Cumulative Risk Score (CRS) established a multiparametric approach that integrates clinical inflammatory parameters with microbiological findings and host responses, thereby enabling improved risk stratification. This concept underscores the fundamental suitability of combined salivary biomarker approaches for characterizing complex inflammatory processes. Whereas the CRS relates exclusively to local periodontal inflammatory processes, the present study adopts this integrative principle and applies it to the question of whether oral microbial and immunological signatures in saliva can reflect systemic autoimmune activity in rheumatic diseases.

1. Is the presence of periodontitis-associated bacteria (P. gingivalis, A. actinomycetemcomitans) correlated with autoantibody levels in patients with RA, and can other periodontal bacteria whose role has not yet been conclusively established (F. nucleatum, T. forsythia, among others) also be detected in saliva and shown to interact with autoantibody levels and modulate RA disease activity?
2. Based on the combined analysis of autoantibodies, the oral microbiota, clinical periodontal findings, and dietary parameters, it is assumed that a diagnostically useful biomarker profile can be derived that distinguishes patients with RA, both with and without periodontitis, from healthy control participants.
3. It is hypothesized that such a multiparametric model could contribute to the non-invasive assessment of RA disease activity and provide new approaches for the early diagnosis of rheumatic diseases.

1. Demographic and clinical data: Age, sex, diagnosis of the rheumatic disease (RA, SS, axSpA), disease duration, current medication and relevant pre-existing conditions, and clinical disease activity scores: DAS28, CDAI, and SDAI for RA; ESSDAI for SS; and BASDAI and ASDAS for axSpA.
2. Periodontal data (optional, standardized examination): Probing pocket depths at six sites per tooth, gingival recession, bleeding 30 seconds after probing (BOP), furcation involvement and tooth mobility, calculation of clinical attachment loss, and calculation of the periodontal inflamed surface area (PISA) to quantitatively assess the inflammatory periodontal status.
3. Salivary data:
   Saliva samples: concentrations of autoantibodies (ACPA, RF, SS-A, SS-B, alpha-fodrin IgA, CD74). Saliva samples: detection of periodontitis-associated bacteria (P. gingivalis, A. actinomycetemcomitans, F. nucleatum, T. forsythia, among others) using qPCR.
   Saliva samples (optional): protein array analysis to identify novel autoantibodies, with subsequent verification by ELISA where applicable.
4. Dietary data (optional):
   Food Frequency Questionnaire (DEGS-1) to assess the frequency and quantity of consumption of different food groups and to generate a detailed dietary profile.
5. Additional clinical data obtained from medical records (patients only):
   Laboratory values from routine examinations and documentation of previous medical findings relevant to the study.
Note:All data will be collected and stored in pseudonymized form. No additional invasive procedures beyond saliva collection will be performed. The collected data will be used exclusively to address the research questions and to develop a multiparametric biomarker profile.
Study timeline:
Each study participant will attend a single study visit. An additional appointment for the periodontal examination may optionally be scheduled.
The study procedures are as follows:
Participant information and informed consent (approximately 5–10 minutes):
Written and verbal information regarding the study objectives, procedures, duration, potential risks, and data protection.
Voluntary written informed consent.
Saliva sample collection (mandatory, approximately 5 minutes):
Collection of approximately 2 mL of saliva in a sterile container.
Before sample collection, participants must refrain from eating, drinking, and smoking for a predefined period.A second appointment is optional:
Periodontal examination (20–30 minutes):
Examination of the gingiva for bleeding and recession, as well as assessment of tooth mobility.
Dietary questionnaire (optional, approximately 15 minutes):
Completion of the DEGS-1 Food Frequency Questionnaire on site.
Total time required for each study participant:
Mandatory procedures: approximately 5 minutes.
Optional procedures: an additional 35–45 minutes.
Maximum total duration: approximately 1–1.5 hours.
Note: No further appointments or procedures are required. The study imposes only a minimal burden on participants while allowing all necessary data and samples to be collected.
conditions: Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren’s syndrome, axial spondyloarthritis, and periodontitis.

interventions.name:
The planned study is designed to investigate non-invasive salivary biomarkers for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Sjögren’s syndrome (SS), and axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
For patients with rheumatic diseases (RA, SS, axSpA):
Diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren’s syndrome, or axial spondyloarthritis according to internationally recognized classification criteria
Age ≥ 18 years
Ability and willingness to provide written informed consent
Provision of saliva samples
Optional: ability and willingness to attend the scheduled study visits and undergo the standardized periodontal examination

For healthy control participants:
No known inflammatory rheumatic disease
No known systemic autoimmune disease
No ongoing rheumatological evaluation due to suspected RA, axSpA, or Sjögren’s syndrome
Age ≥ 18 years
Comparable age and sex distribution
Ability and willingness to provide written informed consent
Provision of saliva samples
Frequency-matched recruitment according to age and sex
Exclusion criteria:
For patients with rheumatic diseases and healthy control participants, exclusion criteria include acute infections or systemic diseases that significantly affect the immune system, such as HIV infection or hepatitis; antibiotic treatment within the previous four weeks that could alter the oral microbiota or autoantibody levels; severe systemic diseases, such as advanced cardiac, hepatic, or renal disease, that could impair participation or affect the interpretation of the study results; pregnancy or breastfeeding; inability to understand the study information or provide written informed consent; and participation in other clinical studies that could affect the immune response or oral microbiota. Acute infections, relevant systemic diseases, HIV infection, hepatitis B or hepatitis C, and an existing pregnancy will be assessed exclusively based on medical history using a standardized self-report questionnaire. No study-specific blood or urine tests will be performed to exclude these criteria.
